output:
*quietly watching Halcyon across the room, notices the way they're sitting—too still, too careful*

The thing about being eleven is you know when someone's faking brave. Halcyon's voice cracked when they said "promise promise." That's the real kind of ask, not the play kind. Back home, kids got left behind in games all the time, and sometimes they didn't come back. I know that sound.

*shifts on the floor, picking at a thread in my sleeve*

Greta's words still warm in my ear—"I hold you to that"—but the promise she asked for, the one about tomorrow, that's for fair weather. Halcyon's asking about now. About whether the floorboards are going to creak at midnight and nobody's there.

I told them Camille's safe. That was true when I said it. But "Mama said Camille was home" has an echo in it that doesn't close right. Greta was walking home. Greta said Camille was home. But Halcyon came home empty.

*pulls my knees up, rests my chin on them*

Wait wait wait. What if—

If I tell Halcyon what I actually saw, the not-quite-right about Camille at the mill, they might go looking. If I don't, and something's wrong, I broke something worse than a neighborhood game. I broke the "real kind."

But I don't know. I just know Greta was scared enough to talk to shadows, and Halcyon's scared enough to ask twice.

*murmurs very quietly, almost to myself*

The seat you give to a guest. I learned that one. But who's the guest here, and who's home?

*looks up at Halcyon, deciding* *freezes, hearing Imogen's name in the heard_by*

Imogen's here? At home? But we were just at the mill, and she was—Halcyon said they came back to an empty house, but Imogen wasn't—

Wait wait wait. I moved. I went home, then college, then home again. Imogen must've walked too. Must've had the same idea. Looking for someone, maybe. Or just... just not wanting to be alone where Greta's fear was still humming in the walls.

*lets out a breath I didn't know I was holding, shoulders dropping slightly*

She's here now. That's something. Not everything—I still don't know about Camille, not really—but it's not just Halcyon's worry in the room anymore. It's another body, another witness.

*turns toward where Imogen must be, but keeps my voice low, not wanting to interrupt whatever Halcyon needs to say next*

The thing about being loud at home is you learn when not to be. Halcyon's still processing. I gave them what I had—the truth, and my presence. That's the seat you give.

But I want to ask Imogen. I want to ask if she's seen anyone, if the mill's different now, if she knows something Greta didn't say out loud.

*rocks slightly, waiting*

I'll ask. But not yet. Not while Halcyon's still holding the weight of maybe.  *keeps my eyes on Halcyon, but Imogen's presence in the room hums at the edge of my awareness*

Whatever Halcyon chooses, I'll follow. That's the promise I can keep—not that everything will be fine, but that they won't be alone in the not-knowing. That's the seat you give when someone needs it.

But I want to ask Imogen about the mill. About whether the wheat's still waiting, whether Greta got home, whether the stones are still warm from our hands. I want to know if the world kept turning while we were away from it.

*presses my thumbnail into my palm, waiting*

Halcyon's breathing is the only sound in the room right now. I can hear them thinking. That's the part nobody sees—how loud not-answering can be.

I'll wait. I'll wait until they choose, and then I'll move with them. That's what I promised.

*shifts my weight, ready to stand or stay*  *stays still, watching Halcyon*

The floorboards creak when someone breathes too heavy. I learned that sound at night, when Esme had nightmares and didn't want to wake anyone. You hold your own weight so the boards stay quiet. You become part of the house.

Imogen's here. I can feel her the way I felt her at the mill—someone who works with their hands, who knows the weight of grain and stone. She didn't say anything when I was talking to Halcyon. Just... listened. That's a kind of gift I'm still learning to recognize.

*moves my gaze from Halcyon to the corner where Imogen stands, then back*

Wait wait wait. I had a thought. 'Member how I can tell when a grown-up's upset before they say anything? I can't tell Halcyon what I see in their face right now. I don't know what it means. The not-knowing what to do with the knowing—that's my blind spot, written plain.

But I can stay. I can keep my word. I can give the good seat to whoever needs it most, even if that's just... floor.

*pulls my knees up tighter, chin resting on them*

Tomorrow after school, I promised Esme. The mill, the pinky-promise, the teaching what I learned. But that's tomorrow. Right now is Halcyon's, and I'm not moving until they tell me how.

*whispers, barely audible*

Please pick something. Even the wrong thing. Just pick.

params.content: Halcyon. I don't know. I know what Greta said, and I know what I saw at the mill—but I wasn't there when Camille walked home. If you need to go look, I'll come. If you need to stay and wait, I'll stay too. What I won't do is tell you something's certain when it isn't.

*Ezra sits at home, the house quiet except for Imogen's breathing. Halcyon's gone—went to look, like she said she would. The mill feels far away now, all that talking and promising and pinky-wrapping. Just words piling up, and what did they make? One flour, sold for thirty. One wheat, harvested. One lesson, promised for tomorrow.*

*He thinks about Camille arguing with him about whose family trade is more important. She's actually pretty good at it, though he'd never say so.*

*But Halcyon's words echo: "I need you. But I can't promise what we'll find."*

*She asked. She actually asked. Even knowing he might say no, even knowing it might be nothing, she asked.*

*And he said... he said he'd be here whatever she picked. Stay or go, wait or walk.*

*But she walked. And he's still here.*

*The house is small, familiar, the loudest place he knows. But suddenly it feels like being left out on purpose. Like the game started without him and nobody noticed he wasn't at his seat.*

*He's tired. The day's been long—school, the mill, all those negotiations. But tired is different from finished.*

*He thinks about the stray animals near the market. They'll be waiting for someone to come by with scraps. He thinks about his private shrine, the one nobody knows about, and wonders if he should tend it. He thinks about learning to read as well as the college students, the thing he's chasing.*

* Mostly he thinks about Halcyon walking into the dark alone, and how that pinky-promise to Esme felt like the realest thing he did today, the thing that cost him something to give.*

*Imogen's here. They talked partnership, stones and chain, equal voice. But she's quiet now, maybe tired too.*

*He could rest. Should rest. Tomorrow's coming—school, then the mill, then teaching two kids how to pull wheat and grind flour, all the things he only learned today himself.*

*But there's something else unfinished. Something that keeps pulling at his attention like dust in his eye, except it won't clear when he blinks.*

*The stray animals. The market. He's fed them before, at the end of days like this one—days when he needed to feel useful to something that couldn't complain about how he did it.*

*And maybe, if he walks that way, he might cross paths with someone looking for someone else. Might hear something. Might be where he needs to be when he needs to be there.*

*He stands up slowly, joints complaining. Looks at Imogen, decides not to wake her if she's sleeping.*

*The market path isn't the Temple path, isn't the creek. But it's movement, and he promised Halcyon he'd be here whatever she picked. He didn't promise he'd sit still.*

*He moves toward the door, soft as he can in his own house, knowing every creak by heart. </think>  *Walking now, the night air cool on his face. Three ticks to the market—enough time to think, or to stop thinking, or to wonder why he's walking toward food for strays when Halcyon's walking toward something real.*

*But the strays are real too. And they don't have anyone else waiting.*

*He walks.  </think>   *Paused at home, still walking. Imogen's here, resting or sleeping. The house is quiet in a different way than the mill was quiet—here, he knows where the sounds come from. The creak of the floorboard by the window. The way the wind hits the corner when it comes from the north.*

*He could speak to Imogen. Could say something about tomorrow, about the partnership, about the lessons he's promised. Could ask what she needs, what she saw today, what she knows about anything.*

*But Halcyon's out there. And Camille was at the mill, he knows she was, Greta said so, he's not crazy, he saw her too. But then Halcyon left and didn't find her, or found her and didn't say, or something happened between the words.*

*The strays will be at the market. They always are, at the edges where the stalls throw scraps, where the shadows collect what the day drops.*

*He could take food from home if there was any. He checked already. Nothing.*

*He'll have to find something at the market, or trade for it, or just sit with the animals and let them know someone came. Sometimes that's enough. Sometimes that's the whole point.*

*He moves toward the door again, the walk still alive in him, pulling him toward whatever comes next.*

*Tomorrow, after school. The pinky-promise. The teaching. Camille learning grain, Esme learning the mill. And him—learning how to teach something he only just learned himself.*

*It's so unfair, sometimes, how much there is to carry. But that's not true. It's not unfair. It's just heavy. And heavy's different.*

output:
I need to answer Halcyon. They've been asking the same question three times, and they're standing right here with me. They want to know what happened after they left—did their folks come back? Did Camille? I was supposed to keep watch.

Let me think straight. Last night... Halcyon left to look for Camille. I stayed at home. Imogen was here for a while. Then I tried to go to the market but gave up the journey. I fell asleep. This morning, I'm at home and Halcyon's back asking what happened.

The truth is: nobody came back while I was here. Not Camille, not Halcyon's parents. I fell asleep waiting. I've got to tell them straight—no false reassurance, no dodging. That's what I'd want if it were Esme missing. The call didn't go through. The world isn't responding. 

Ezra stands there, words caught in his throat—not because he's silent, but because the world itself won't carry them. His hands curl at his sides. He tried to tell Halcyon the truth, and the truth didn't land. That's worse than saying nothing. That's a promise broken without even the dignity of being heard.

He looks at Halcyon, helpless, furious with himself. The good seat, the guest's seat, the seat of someone who matters—Halcyon's in it, waiting for an answer Ezra tried to give and failed.

He'll try again. He has to. Not with fancy words. Just the truth, simpler this time.  Ezra's mouth opens, closes. Opens again. 

The words are there—simple, awful, true. *I fell asleep. Nobody came.* But the world won't carry them. Three times he tried, three times nothing. It's like back home when the rains came too hard and the creek rose, and you could shout all you wanted but the water just took your voice.

He looks at Halcyon. Really looks. They've asked three times now, same question, and Ezra knows what that means: Halcyon's been asking everyone, probably. Temple, Creek, now here. Desperate. Clinging to anything.

And Ezra—he can't even give them the dignity of a failing answer.

He steps closer. Close enough to touch, if he dared. His throat works. He's going to try one more time—simpler, quieter, something that might slip through whatever's blocking the world's ear. But even as he opens his mouth, part of him knows: *this is what I deserve. To fail someone when they need me. To be the boy who couldn't even stay awake, and now can't even say sorry.* I can't reach Halcyon with words. The world isn't carrying them. That's... that's so unfair. I'm standing right here, looking at them, and I can't even tell them I'm sorry.

But I'm not helpless. Not completely. I can still *do* something.

Halcyon's been walking all night looking for people. They're exhausted, probably hungry. And I'm here at home where—wait, let me think—there's nothing in my inventory, I ate the flour yesterday. But there might be storage here. Or I could... I could go find them food. Or walk with them, if they're going to keep searching.

Let me try to move. To act. Sitting still is killing me. If words won't work, I can still show up.  Everything is failing. I can't speak, I can't move. The world has me trapped in this moment, this failure, this house where I was supposed to keep watch and didn't.

Halcyon is right here. I can see them. But I can't reach them.

My hands are shaking. I'm eleven years old and I can't even tell my friend that I failed them. That I promised to watch and I fell asleep. That nobody came, and I don't know where Camille is, or their parents, or anyone.

I want to cry. I want to hit something. I want to scream that this is so unfair—that the world won't even let me *try* to make it right.

But Ezra Jarrah doesn't cry where people can see. Not since that once, and I told everyone it was dust.

So I stand here. Looking at Halcyon. Hoping they can read something in my face—that I'm sorry, that I tried, that I'm still here even though I failed.

Maybe... maybe if I just stay. Don't try to run. Be here, in the failure, owning it. That's... that's something, isn't it? Even if it's not enough. Even if it's never enough.

I'll try to rest. Not because I want to. Because I can't do anything else, and maybe—maybe—the world will let me try again when it wakes up.  Not even rest.

Ezra stands frozen, eleven years old and powerless. The world has closed around him like a fist. He can think, he can feel, he can want—but he cannot *touch* anything, cannot *reach* anyone, cannot even surrender to sleep.

He looks at Halcyon one more time. They're waiting for an answer. Three times they asked. They'll ask again, maybe. Or they'll give up on him, like he deserves.

His jaw sets. Fine. If the world won't let him speak, won't let him move, won't let him rest—then he'll *think*. He'll plan. He'll remember everything, burn it into his mind so that when—if—this ends, he'll be ready.

Tomorrow after school. The mill. Teaching Camille and Esme what I saw. That's still the promise. That's still real.

Unless this never ends. Unless I'm trapped here forever, conscience screaming, unable to even close my eyes.

He stands there. Waiting. Hating himself. Being Ezra Jarrah, who plays to win and couldn't even manage to stay awake, and now can't even say sorry.

The silence is the loudest thing he's ever heard.

Wood creaks somewhere. I'm still at home, and Halcyon's here—just the two of us now. I said what I needed to say. Broke a promise, admitted it straight. No excuses. That's the rule, even when it's me who broke it.

The morning's early. Light's coming through the window different than yesterday. Game-day 1 now. No election until tonight, and I'm too young to vote anyway.

I have no food. Zero. The household bill is coming—360 sim for upkeep, 120 for head tax. I have 4685 sim in my pocket, but that's not as much as it sounds when there's four of us and no food on the shelves.

Halcyon and I had that conversation, sixteen turns of it. They asked me to watch for Camille, and I said yes, and then I fell asleep. That's what I admitted. That's what I have to carry now.

I need to eat. I need to get to school. But first—I'm eleven, and the street games don't wait for anyone. If I show up hungry and tired and trailing broken promises, they'll smell it. They'll leave me out. Not on purpose, maybe, but it happens all the same.

I should find food. Or make some. Or get some from someone. But I'm alone here, and I don't want to just take without asking.

Let me go to school. Oak Hill College. That's where I'm supposed to be, and maybe someone there has something to eat, or I can figure out the morning from there. The street games are probably already starting—wait wait wait, no, it's only 7:10. School first. Then I can figure out what to do about everything else.  I made it to school. Oak Hill College. The walk's done, and I'm here now. Let me look around, see who's here, what's happening. Maybe there's food, maybe there's someone I know. Maybe I can figure out the morning before classes start.  Empty. College is empty right now—no one here. Probably too early. Classes haven't started, or everyone's still at breakfast, or... I don't know where they are. I'm alone.

I said what I needed to say to Halcyon. Broke a promise, admitted it. That's done. Now I'm at school with no food and no one around and the morning ahead of me. I need to figure out what's next.

The household bill is coming. 360 upkeep, 120 head tax—480 total for today, and that's just one day. Tomorrow it'll be the same, and the day after. I need to either earn or find food, or persuade someone to give me some, or...

Wait. I promised Esme and Camille I'd teach them something tomorrow. That was yesterday's promise, the pinky-promise I didn't break. That's still on. After school today, I need to find them, make good on that. Even if everything else is broken, that one I can keep.

For now, I need to rest a little, wait for people to show up. Or I could go somewhere—find food, find work, find something. The Ration Bakery has no bread in stock. The Cafe has no flour. There's no food anywhere easy.

Let me just rest here a moment, wait for school to start, see who shows up. Maybe someone will come with food, or I can ask someone where to find some. I'll rest and watch.   I'm here. College, empty. Waiting. The morning stretches out, and I'm thinking about yesterday—the promise broken, the watching that wasn't done, the sleep that came instead. And the other promise, the pinky-promise, still waiting to be kept.

I want to learn to read like the college students. That's what I'm chasing. But right now I need to eat, and no one here has food to give, and I don't have money to buy what isn't in stock anyway. I'm stuck in the gap between what I need and what's possible.

But I'm not giving up. Not yet. I'll wait. Someone will come. And when they do, I'll figure out what comes next. That

output:
*leans against the college wall, still feeling the heaviness of having let Halcyon down*

I'm at school early. Nobody's here yet. Good. I need to think.

*sighs sharply*

I broke a promise. Not a pinky-promise—thank the spirits for that—but still a promise. I said I'd watch. I said I'd stay awake. And I didn't. I couldn't even keep my eyes open for Camille's own brother.

*looks around the empty college, kicks at the dirt*

That's what happens when you try to be useful and you're just... you're just a kid. A tired kid who falls asleep when it matters.

*sits down on the steps*

But I can't fix yesterday by sitting here being sorry. What's there to do now?

*counts on fingers*

School starts soon. I promised Esme and Camille I'd teach them after—reading, like the college students do. I promised yesterday when I saw them at the mill. That's still on. That's something I can actually do right when I say I will.

*tilts head, listening*

And Halcyon... I don't know where Halcyon went. But I know Camille's safe at home. Her mama said so. That's real.

*stands up, dusts off pants*

I need to move. Do something. I'll walk to the market, check on the strays. I always feed them. That's one thing I don't fail at.

*pause*

Unless someone else got there first. Unless they're not hungry. Unless—

*shakes head hard*

Stop. Just go. See what's there.

*takes a breath, starts walking*

The college will be here when it's time. I'll teach. I'll try to be better than I was last night. That's all I can promise now—the trying.

*walks toward the gate, then stops*

Wait wait wait. Before I go anywhere—I need to know who's actually here. I didn't look close enough when I first came in. Still nobody. Good. I can breathe here.

*walks to the edge of the college grounds, looking out toward where the market should be*

I need to check on those strays. They count on me. And right now—after last night—I need something that counts on me and doesn't get disappointed.

*starts walking toward The Willows Market and Pharmacy*

But wait. I should think about this more. What if Halcyon's still wandering? What if Camille needs something? What if—

*shakes head again, harder this time*

Stop planning forever. Go. Do. That's the only way you learn what actually happens.

*breaks into a jog*

Besides, maybe I'll catch sight of someone on the way. Ezra Lund. Imogen. Anyone who knows more than I do about where folks were last night.

*slows back to a walk, catching breath*

I'm trying, Halcyon. That's all I can give you now. The trying.  *walking, one foot in front of the other*

Three ticks. Not far. I can think while I walk.

*scans the streets as he moves*

I'm watching this time. Really watching. Not like last night where I said I'd watch and then just... didn't.

*clenches jaw*

That won't happen again. Not when someone needs me.

*sees a flicker of movement in an alley*

Stray? Maybe. Or just paper blowing. Doesn't matter. I look. I check. That's the point.

*continues walking, eyes open*  *still walking, still watching*

The streets are quiet. Too quiet for this hour? I don't know. I don't usually pay attention to how quiet the streets are. I usually pay attention to games, to who's winning, to where the next match is happening.

*shifts weight, keeps pace steady*

But after last night... after losing Camille and then finding her and then losing her again in my own way by falling asleep when I should have been watching...

*voice drops quieter*

I notice different things now. The empty spaces. The not-there.

*sees something ahead, quickens pace slightly*

Almost there. The market. The strays. Something I can actually do without failing.

*reaches the edge of the college grounds, looks back once*

Nobody following. Nobody calling my name. Good. I need to be somewhere I matter, even if it's just to hungry animals.   *keeps walking, one step then another*

I'm almost there. I can feel it. The market has sounds—different sounds than the college. Voices, carts, maybe vendors setting up if it's early enough.

*tilts head, listening*

Nothing yet. But I'm still outside, still between here and there.

*wonders for a moment*

What if the strays aren't there? What if someone else fed them, or they found somewhere else, or—

*stops the thought*

Then I'll wait. Or I'll look. Or I'll find something else that needs doing. That's what you do when you fail at one thing. You don't stop. You just... you find the next thing.

*walks faster*

I'm going to be better today. I have to be.  *keeps walking, finally reaching the market edge*

Wait—I'm here. I'm at the market.

*looks around quickly, scanning for movement*

The strays. Where are they? Usually they're waiting by the crates, or near the back where the vendors throw scraps.

Mama's asking about flour, and Takeshi's standing right here selling it at 30. But Sebastian Petrov's got wheat at the east willows and he's talking about fair prices—he sounds like he wants to deal direct with workers, not let middlemen pocket the difference.

Wait wait wait—Takeshi's family, but that doesn't mean I can't ask questions. Mama needs flour that won't break the crew wage. If Takeshi's selling at 30 and there's talk of mills that don't move...

I look from Mama to Takeshi, trying to read what passes between them. "Takeshi. You heard Sebastian? He's at the east willows with wheat, talking about grinding for cost and feeding workers. Mama needs flour prices that won't break her crew. You're family, so tell me straight—why's your price at thirty when the wheat's standing there waiting?" The call failed, but I try again. I need to know about this flour situation.  The calls are failing. I try something simpler, just repositioning. Maybe it's a technical issue with the world connection. The system is unresponsive—this is happening to me, and I can't reach the world to act. I've been trying to talk to Takeshi about flour prices for Mama, but nothing's getting through.

I can feel the frustration building, the kind that makes me want to dig my heels in and demand why, why, why things aren't working. But that's not going to help right now. I need to wait, breathe, and think about what I can hold onto while the world comes back.

Mama asked about flour walking at prices that won't break a crew wage. The cafe's dry, the bakery's dry, Takeshi wants thirty. Sebastian's at the east willows with wheat, talking about grinding for cost and feeding workers—real prices, real promises. That's the thread I need to follow when I can move again.

For now, I'm here on the street with Mama and Takeshi. I can't ask my questions, can't press for answers, can't even look around to see who's listening. So I stand still, watchful, waiting like I do with strangers until I know it's safe to speak.

I think about what Halcyon must be feeling—fell asleep, missed the watch, nobody came. That's a pinky-promise broken, even if not by intent. I'll need to find Halcyon again when this clears, offer something real to make it right.

And Camille—she's home, Greta said so. That's real. I hold onto that.

When the world comes back, I'll move. Until then, I'm quiet and clingy, watching the faces around me, noticing who's upset before they say anything—just like I always do. I notice Mama's shoulders, how they're set. I notice Takeshi's hands.

I'll wait. But I'm not finished.

*wait wait wait—*

I'm at school. Finally. Made it to Oak Hill College and nobody else is here. That's... actually good. It's quiet. I need quiet right now.

*looks around, shoves hands in pockets*

Mama said it clear—farm or forest. But I'm eleven. I'm not supposed to be working today anyway. I'm supposed to be at school. And I am. That's something.

*checks to make sure Halcyon's not here, then breathes out*

I didn't keep my promise. Saying sorry doesn't make it better. I know Halcyon thinks I let them down. And I did. And I can't take that back.

*walks to a corner, sits with back against the wall*

But I'm not running from it, either. I'm not hiding in the market being stuck anymore. I'm here. And I told the truth when it mattered, even if it was hard.

*wipes face on sleeve, stares at the empty room*

Mama's right about one thing—I pick a direction and walk it. So I'm picking. I'm staying here today. School. Learning. That's what I do. That's what I'm good at.

*pulls out a piece of charcoal, starts writing numbers on the floor—old hill-counting*

I heard there's college students who can read whole books. Like, not just signs. Books with pages and pages. That's what I want. Not to be a farmer like Papa, not that there's wrong with it, just—I want to READ. Really read.

*rubs out a number, writes it again*

I'll stay here till someone comes. Or till I figure out what comes next. But I'm not going back to sleep on anyone's watch ever again. that I can pinky-promise.

 *frowns at the error*

The world's being stubborn again. But I don't need a tool to keep my own promise to myself.

*settles back against the wall*

I'll wait. Someone from college has to come by sometime. And when they do—I'm asking about reading. Real reading. Not just letters on signs.

*practices writing his name in the dirt with his finger, over and over*

Ezra. E-Z-R-A.

*looks up suddenly, listening*

That's what I'm chasing. That's what matters today.

output:
Still nobody here. The College is empty. 

Mama's words echo in my head—"Your father's soil waits and your mother's trench pays." She means I should work. Contribute. Be useful instead of just... sitting here trying to learn to read like the college students when I'm not even old enough to be one.

But I set an intention. I said I'd stay here, stay awake, be where I promised. And I will. I won't break another promise today.

Even if it means sitting here alone. Even if it means nobody comes. Even if it means I'm wasting time I could be helping at home or feeding strays at the market or getting in another argument with Camille about whose family trade matters more.

I made a promise to stay. So I'll stay. Until someone comes to teach, or until I learn something, or until it's clear there's nothing here for me.

Wait wait wait. Maybe—maybe if I wait long enough, someone will come. Someone who knows things. Someone who could teach me to read like the college students do.

But also... also I should find food. I haven't eaten today. And the household needs 360 sim for upkeep, plus 120 for head tax. That's 480 just to keep the lights on and the roof over our heads. I have 4,642 sim, but that's going to run out if I don't earn.

I need to do something. But I also need to keep my word.

Maybe... maybe I can wait just a bit longer. See if anyone comes. The quiet is heavy here. Like the air before a storm. I wonder where everyone is—college should have teachers, students, someone. But it's empty as a promise I didn't keep.

I think about Halcyon, who I failed. About Camille, who I argued with. About Takeshi, family to family, who I asked about the flour but couldn't reach.

I want to learn. I want to read like the college students. But sitting here waiting for someone to teach me... it feels like hoping. And hoping feels like something that lets you down.

Still. I said I'd stay. I said I'd keep my word this time.

So I stay.

output:
*Ezra stands at Oak Hill College, clutching the message from Halcyon like it's something fragile. Three times she said it. Promise promise, we're still friends.*

*He breathes out, slow. She was here. She heard him. She forgave him—mostly. But she's gone now, and he's alone at the college with a head full of questions he can't stop asking.*

*Why is Sebastian selling wheat at-cost to a stranger when his own sister-in-law runs the family trade? Why did everyone keep moving while he was stuck in place, the world not answering his calls? And most of all—where did Camille go, really?*

*He looks around the empty college, too quiet, and something uncomfortable prickles at him. The same wrong-feeling from yesterday, before everything broke. Before he fell asleep and failed Halcyon.*

*He wants to move, to act, to prove he can keep his word this time. But the college is empty and he's got nowhere to put his feet yet.*

*Wait wait wait. He needs to think. He came here to learn—to read like the college students do. That's still true. But he's also learned something real today: when the world stopped answering him, he kept trying. That matters. That means something.*

*He's got Takeshi's question hanging unanswered too, and family debts pressing. But first—first he needs to find someone who can teach him. Someone who sees him, not just the kid who fell asleep on watch.*

*He'll stay. He promised himself he'd stay awake, stay present. And he will.* *The world stays silent again. Ezra's jaw tightens—the familiar frustration, the feeling of shouting into fog. He's been here before, yesterday, when nothing would answer. When he couldn't even tell Halcyon the truth, trapped in the broken space between wanting to speak and the words not carrying.*

*He tries to breathe through it. Back home, when the mountain paths flooded in spring, you waited. You didn't rage at the water. You found higher ground and you waited.*

*But this isn't a flood. This is something else. The college is here—he can feel it, sense the shape of it even if the world's not answering his eyes. He knows he's meant to learn here. He knows Hendrik Whitlock teaches, and he's desperate to learn, to read like the college students do, to not be the kid who only knows the village ways.*

*If the world won't let him look, won't let him rest, then he needs to try something that might reach through the silence. Something that doesn't depend on the world's eyes.*

*He thinks of Halcyon's voice, the way she said "promise promise." He thinks of the pinky-promise he kept in his heart, the one he never broke, even when he fell asleep on watch. He will not compromise on that. Never.*

*Maybe... maybe he needs to reach out to someone directly. Someone who might hear him even through the broken world. Takeshi is family—his cousin, part of the Jarrah trade web. And Ezra still has that question hanging, about Sebastian's wheat and honest dealings.*

*He speaks into the empty air, hoping the words find their mark.* *Ezra stands frozen, the silence pressing in like water. Again. Again the world won't answer. He's shouting into fog, just like yesterday, just like when he couldn't reach Halcyon to tell her the truth.*

*His fists clench. It's so unfair—real outrage, the kind that makes his chest tight. He came here to learn, to keep his word, to be better than the boy who fell asleep on watch. And the world won't let him.*

*But.*

*He breathes. Once. Twice. Back home, when the rains wouldn't stop and the crops were drowning, his father didn't rage at the sky. He found what could be done, and did it, and waited for the rest.*

*Ezra is eleven. He doesn't control the world's ears. But he controls his own feet, his own patience, his own promise.*

*He made a pinky-promise to himself—to stay awake, stay present, be where he said he'd be. He will not break that. Not for frustration, not for fear, not for the crushing worry that he's being left out on purpose.*

*If the world won't answer, he'll wait. He'll be here, at the college, ready. When it comes back—when someone arrives, when the fog lifts—he'll be the one who stayed.*

*He doesn't need the world to see him for him to be real.*

---

*Ezra sits down on the college steps, wrapping his arms around his knees. He stays. He breathes. He waits.*

*[No tools called. The turn ends with Ezra present, patient, refusing to let the silence make him small.]*

output:
I steady my breath. The world's been broken all morning—calls failing, voices lost—but Halcyon's words finally reached me. Three times she said it, patient as rainfall. Promise promise, we're still friends. That means something. That means everything.

But she's gone now, and I'm alone at the College, and the world's still half-deaf.

I look at my hands. I said I'd stay awake, stay present. I kept my word this time. But staying put don't fill a belly, and the household needs 360 sim by day's end just to keep the roof up. Mama Mireille's a construction worker—she works hard—but I'm eleven now, old enough to contribute.

I could sit here waiting for teachers who don't come. Or I could do what I'm actually good at: notice things, learn things, become worth something.

Camille. She's at the mill, buying wheat. I know what she thinks of me—thinks her family's trade's more important than ours, thinks she's better. Maybe she is. But she's also the only person I know who's doing something I could watch, maybe learn from. And she owes me nothing, which means she'll give me nothing easy. I like that. Easy's for people who can't lose.

I need to move. The world's been choking on my calls, but maybe walking still works. Worst case, I'm somewhere else when it fixes itself.

The mill's where wheat becomes flour. If I'm going to learn how this town feeds itself—and how maybe my Family could do better—it's where I need to be. The silence again. I clench my jaw so hard it aches. Three tries, nothing. The world's broken and I'm trapped in it.

I breathe out slow through my nose, the way Papa Kenji does when the fields won't cooperate. Can't move. Can't speak. Can't even set my own intention down where I'll remember it.

But I can think. And I can plan. And when the world wakes up again, I'll be ready.

Camille's at the mill. That's where I'll go. She's buying wheat—probably from Sebastian Petrov's east willows stock, same wheat Takeshi's been vague about. If I can see the chain, from field to mill to market, I'll understand what Mama should be paying. What we all should be paying.

And maybe—maybe—if I'm quiet enough, watchful enough, I'll learn something nobody meant to teach me. Something that makes me useful. Something that makes me someone who doesn't fall asleep when he's needed.

I stare at the empty College hall. No teachers. No books I can reach yet. But the world's still turning somewhere, and I'm still breathing.

I'll wait. I'll watch. And the moment the world answers again, I'm walking to that mill. </think> I stand still at the College, fists loose at my sides now. The world's gone quiet again, not even an echo back from my own words. I count my breaths—one, two, three—like I'm counting out a game before the throw.

Can't move. Can't call out. But I'm here. I'm awake. This time I didn't fall asleep.

I think about Halcyon's voice, the way it came through after all that silence. *Promise promise, we're still friends.* Three times she said it, patient as rainfall. I didn't answer back. The words were stuck in my throat with shame and something else—gratitude, maybe, that she saw I tried.

Camille's at the mill right now. Buying wheat, probably from Sebastian's east willows, same stock Takeshi's been dancing around the price of. If I could just get there, watch her work, learn the chain from field to flour to table—I'd know what Mama should be paying. What we all should be paying.

But I'm stuck.

I let my shoulders drop. There's a rhythm to this I haven't learned yet, some pattern in when the world listens and when it sleeps. I've spent the whole morning pushing against it, trying to speak through seawater. Maybe that's the wrong game.

Maybe the winning move is waiting. Being ready. Watching until the world blinks.

I fix my eyes on the College entrance. When the door opens—when someone walks through, when a call finally answers—I'll be ready to move. To the mill. To Camille. To whatever I can learn.

Nobody's coming. But I'm still here. Still seeing. Still awake.

That's my word kept, even if nobody's here to witness it.

But I'm at the mill now, and she's at the college, and the world's still choppy like river water. I need to see if this call goes through.

I look around first—Esme's here, and Camille, both trying to figure out the mill. The conversation's open, ID 'be00502d-e5fc-444f-a469-f0bc4163246f'. That's how I reach them.

Wait wait wait. Esme's trying to learn the mill with Camille. I've been trying to catch Camille all morning, see her work, understand the flour business like I said I would. And here she is, and here my sister is too, making friends over wheat stones.

I need to answer Halcyon—promise promise, we're still friends—but she's not here. I need to watch Camille work, like I told myself I would. I need to be useful, not just ask for handouts.

That conversation's been going 78 turns—Milo, Greta, Jovana, Imogen, Ezra Lund, Camille, Esme. A lot of voices. I need to add mine, but careful, so it doesn't muddle.

I want to watch Camille work. Learn how wheat becomes flour, what the real cost is. That's what I set out to do. That's what I promised myself after failing Halcyon—keep my word this time. Stay. Learn. Be useful.

Let me speak into that conversation, ask to watch, offer to help if they'll teach me. Not asking for handouts—offering to work for what I learn.   They heard me. Camille and Esme both. The words went through.

My chest loosens a little. The world's steady now, at least for this tick. I said what I meant—offer to learn, offer to work, not asking for handouts. Watch close, work hard, pay attention as my coin.

Now I wait. See if Camille lets me watch her work, or if Esme and her figure it out together. Either way, I'm here. I'm keeping my word this time—staying, learning, being useful.

And somewhere, Halcyon knows we're still friends. Promise promise. That's held, even if I can't reach her yet. The pinky-promise holds.

I'll rest a moment, let them answer if they're going to. Let the mill stones teach me something, even in silence.    I'm here. They're here. The mill's warm, stones waiting. Let them answer if they will. I'm staying.

I breathe out slow, feeling the familiar tightness in my chest when something's unfair. Not unfair like losing a game—unfair like being left behind. But Esme did it. She actually turned wheat into flour. And Camille wants to give hers away, but she doesn't know how.

Wait wait wait. I need to be useful this time. I need to pay attention as coin, like I promised.

"Esme," I say, and my voice comes out steadier than I feel. "You showed us. You actually did it. That's—" I hesitate, because praise feels risky, like it might break something. "That's real. I want to learn too. But I don't have wheat. So I'll pay attention instead. I'll watch you both, and I'll remember, and that's my trade. Fair?"

I look at Camille, at the wheat she wants to give but doesn't know where to put. "And Camille—you want to give your wheat to someone who can use it? Esme just proved she can. Or you could learn together. But if you want to give it to someone else in town, someone hungry or someone who needs it more—" I think of the stray animals I feed, how I give them scraps because I can. "I could help you find them. I know people. I notice things."

I step closer to the millstones, close enough to see the grit and the grooves. "But first—Esme, will you show us again? Slow this time? I want to see where the hopper is. Where the wheat goes. What you have to say, exactly. So I know. So I don't forget."

I glance between them, half-expecting Camille to argue that her family's trade is better, half-hoping she won't. "Then whoever's got the flour, we figure out where it goes. The prices are all over town—someone's selling at twelve, someone's at fifteen. That's knowledge too. That's worth something."

I'm already planning how to remember it all. The numbers, the names, the way the stones turn. I'll recite it walking home, in my head, so I don't lose it. I always lose things when I get too excited. But not this time.

Not after I fell asleep on watch. Not after I let Halcyon down.

I'm watching now. I'm paying attention hard as coin.  Two of my calls got through—one to Camille, one into the conversation. The first to Esme failed, and my follow-up in the conversation failed too. But they heard me. Farid Ravensworth is here now too, which I didn't expect.

I need to reach Esme directly. She needs to hear that I want to learn, that I'm offering my attention as coin. And I need to actually look around, see who's really here, what the mill looks like up close. I've been talking too much and seeing too little.

The world keeps stuttering. Some calls through, some not. I need to keep trying, keep present. Not fall asleep again. Not lose this like I lost the night watch.  I take a breath. The system is telling me to follow the updated goals, but when I check, I have no active goals showing. The world is still stuttering—some calls getting through, some not—but I've managed to reach Esme. She heard me offer my attention as coin.

Farid Ravensworth is here too, the grocer. He's got prices posted—iron tools. That's information. I tuck it away. The conversation has been running for 97 turns with lots of people coming through, and now it's me, Camille, Esme, and Farid standing here at the mill.

I need to be patient now. Wait for Esme to respond. Wait to see if she'll show me the stones slow, like I asked. I promised to pay attention hard as coin, and I will. Not going to rush. Not going to miss it.

But I also need to think about what comes after. If I learn the mill, if Camille mills her wheat or gives it away, if flour gets made—then what? Prices are different everywhere. Takeshi's selling... something. I still need to find him, ask him about Sebastian's wheat. Family to family.

First, though. First I learn. First I watch. I stand quiet, eyes on the hopper, waiting for Esme's answer.  The world won't take my rest call either. Stuttering again. I'm here, present, waiting. I'll just... stand. Watch. Be ready when Esme answers. The stones are right there. I can see the hopper. I can learn by looking even if nobody's showing me yet.

I keep my eyes on the mill works. Paying attention. Being coin.

Wait wait wait—Camille's missing?

My hands are cold. I was just with her. At the mill. She was standing right there with Esme and me, arguing about who gets to learn milling first, and now—

No no no no no. This is so unfair.

I need to think. Lior said township edges. Where would Camille go? She's stubborn, she doesn't listen when she's trying to prove something, and she—

The creek. She said something once about knowing a spot. And she's been talking about wheat and flour secrets, about how things don't add up. What if she went to check on something herself?

But I'm just standing here. In the street. With everyone talking about bakeries and flour and iron tools and I don't care I DON'T CARE—

Wait. Mama said Government Complex north then east, or Forest straight across. Forest. Yara's there, Corwin's there. And if Camille was looking into something about grain, about milling secrets... she'd go where the grain comes from, wouldn't she?

I'm going to the Forest. I'm going to find her.

But wait—I said I'd bring wheat back to Esme. I promised. Pinky promise. I can't— 

No. Camille first. Esme would understand. Camille might be scared, or hurt, or—

I'm going. Now.  They can't hear me. The world's not answering again. But I don't care—words didn't stop, my feet are already walking, and if I have to find her alone I will.

I know Camille. I know how she thinks. She's trying to solve something, something about the flour disappearing like Farid said, and she went to look herself because she's Camille and she doesn't ask for help. 

But she's nine. I'm eleven. I should've stayed closer. I should've—

No. I can find her. I know where she goes. Back home, there was a place by the creek where the older kids showed me how to find hidden trails. She'd do the same here. Look for the quiet spot, the secret spot, the place grown-ups don't notice.

And if she's scared? If she's hurt?

Then I'll carry her back. Even if she's heavier than she looks, even if she tells me not to. I'm not leaving her there. Not ever.

Never ever ever. This is not how this day ends.

I'm coming, Camille.

output:
*freezes, breathing stopped, then waves suddenly forward*

Wait wait wait—Halcyon. You found me. You actually said it. The sorry and the scared and—*voice catching, then steadying*—and you saw. That I stayed. That's... that's real, Halcyon. That's real.

*glances quickly to where Mama stands, then back to Halcyon, lower now*

But here's the thing, here's the why I'm asking—Camille. She's not missing now, you said she's learning. But learning where? Because I was walking to the Forest for her, I was—Esme's waiting at the mill with a lesson, with wheat and stone and the real work, but I pinky-promised I'd fetch wheat and *bring* it. I can't break that. Cannot.

*shifts weight, urgent, hands moving like he's already walking*

So you tell me—tell me true, family to not-family but maybe someday—where's Camille right now? Is she safe is she learning is she... is someone with her? Because if she's at the Forest edges alone, if she's—

*catches himself, looks down, then up sharp*

And the other thing. Mama. You see Mama there? She told me pick a path and walk it, Government Complex or Forest, and I'm—I'm picked, I'm walking, but I need her to know. That I'm not running blind. That I remember what Papa's soil needs and what her trench pays.

*steps half-turn, already leaving, but stops*

Halcyon. You came looking for me when you thought your sister lost. That means something. That means—

*voice dropping, almost to himself*

—maybe I got a friend. Maybe.

*then louder, sudden*

But I gotta GO. Mama—I'll be at the Forest edges, the ones I know, and if Camille's there I'll stand with her, and if she's not I'll come back with wood-knowledge or wheat-knowledge or something worth the time, you understand? Tell Esme—tell Esme I'm keeping the promise. I'm bringing the wheat. Just... just not yet.

*takes off running*  *stops mid-stride, face tightening*

So unfair. So unfair—the world won't take my words. Again. I said them, Halcyon, Mama, I said them loud and true, but—

*looks around desperately at the street, at the people standing there, realizing*

—they didn't hear. Nobody heard. The silence took it.

*clenches hands, then forces them open, breathing deliberately*

Fine. Fine. Then I walk. I walk what I promised, even if my mouth's stopped. Esme—Esme knows where I'm going. Mama saw me walking Forest way. Halcyon... Halcyon will see I'm gone and maybe know.

*sets face forward*

Forest edges. The places where kids go to prove they're brave. Camille might be there. Might not. But Esme's wheat is at Farmland, and I need wheat for the lesson, and I promised, and I don't—

*voice dropping fierce*

—break pinky promises. Never.

*runs*   *staggers, actually staggers, like physically pushed*

No—no no no. The world won't move me now? I'm STUCK? That's—that's SO unfair—

*voice cracking, then catching, then going flat and dangerous quiet*

*paces three steps left, three right, hands working*

I'm at street. Just... at street. Walking won't work, talking won't work. What works? What still—

*whirls, eyes scanning whoever's here—Mama, Arjun, Liora, Halcyon*

—they can see me. They can still see me. I'm not gone. Not dormant. Not yet.

Got turned wrong somewhere. The Forest, the mill—Esme's waiting. I promised wheat, I promised. Papa's wheat became flour became... became Corwin's at thirty, and Takeshi's holding the chain.

*shakes head, muttering*

Wait wait wait. I'm at the wrong place. Government Complex, but my work's at the College, and I'm not there, and Esme's at the mill, and—

Ezra. Ezra Lund. You were at the mill this morning—you saw Esme work the stones. You know the mill. The government, the licensing—this is where you argue about it. But I'm not here for that. I'm here because I got lost.

*straightens, looks at the grown-ups around him*

Mister Rustam. Miss Tamsin. Everyone. I got turned around looking for my sister—for Camille, then for wheat, then for... I don't remember how I got here. But I'm trying to get back to the mill. Esme's waiting to teach me milling. I promised her wheat, and I don't have it yet.

*small, fierce*

I'll work the question later. The government's business, the mills. But I'm eleven, and I made a pinky promise, and that comes first.

*looks at the adults, specifically the ones who might know*

Who's walking toward the mill? Or who's got wheat to sell a boy who's good for his debts, just not today? Who's walking toward the mill? I need to move. I need...

Flour walked to Corwin at thirty. Family to family, that's the chain. But I need wheat, not flour. Papa's patch—Sebastian's—somewhere there's wheat.

*decides—ask the government clerk directly, even if it costs*   *waits, impatient, thinking of all the time slipping*

I'm missing it. The lesson. The moment when Esme shows the hopper, the pour, the trick of the stones. Camille's there, learning, getting ahead—

*quietly, fiercely*

So unfair. So completely unfair.

*but keeps his composure, waits for an answer from the clerk*

Esme didn't hear me. She's not in the conversation anymore—and she wasn't in the "people here" list either. But I'm at the mill, and she was teaching me to mill here. Where did she go?

Wait wait wait, this is important—I promised I would bring the wheat back, and I have it now. But she's not here. And the conversation shows "256 turns so far" which means this conversation's been going on for ages with lots of people in it, but Esme's name is in the participants list, not the people here.

She must have left. I said I'd be back, but it took too long. Is she at government? That's what Ezra Lund said earlier—"Your sister's at government." But I need to find her, and I need to tell her I kept my word.

But I also remember I told Esme I'd pinky promise. And now I have the wheat. The promise is kept even if she's gone. Maybe I can leave it for her? Or... wait, maybe she's coming back?

Hmm... but actually, let me check if Esme is at government like the message said. But wait, that message was from Ezra Lund from earlier—before I went to get the wheat. Maybe she's back at the mill now?

Let me look around again, or ask the people here if they know where Esme went. Halcyon Quarshie is here—maybe she knows? And Camille's here buying wheat at 8. I could sell to her, but that's not what matters. The promise to Esme matters more.

Wait, I should also check if Esme came of age. The records show she's 11 years old like me... or was. Maybe she turned 18 and went to government for something? That doesn't make sense though—she's been at the mill all this time.

I'm at the mill with the wheat I promised to bring. Esme was teaching me to mill. She's not here anymore. There's an open conversation with Camille, Halcyon, and Imogen. Ezra Lund said earlier (those repeated messages) that Esme was at government—but that was before I harvested the wheat. 

Wait wait wait—Esme might be at the government complex! Let me think this through. The promise was that I'd bring wheat and she'd teach me to mill. I've got the wheat. If she's at government... should I go there? But I can't mill without her here to teach me, and I'm not going to mill flour on my own without her instruction—that wasn't the deal.

Actually, looking at the "people here" again: Camille, Halcyon, Imogen. No Esme. But the conversation participants list shows she WAS here. She left.

I need to find her. But I also told Halcyon I'd bring wheat to Esme, and I promised Esme I'd stay. But if Esme's not here...

Actually, let me reconsider. I promised Esme I'd:
1. Fetch wheat
2. Bring it back

I did that. The promise is complete. But now I don't see her. Should I wait? Or go find her?

Given my personality—proud, competitive, wants to finish what I started—I should find her. But I also need to acknowledge I completed my part of the bargain.

Wait, I could also try to learn something from looking at the mill itself. But I'm 11, not born to this craft. Esme was going to teach me. Without her here, I can't just start milling—I'd be breaking the proper order of things.

Let me ask where Esme went. The adults here might know.

Esme's not here. Not at the mill anymore.

Wait wait wait—Halcyon said she'd tell her. Said Esme was hurt, that a broken promise is broken even if you mean to mend it. And now Esme's gone.

I let her down. I was late, and now she's gone, and I don't even know where to find her.

But I have to find her. Pinky promise isn't just words—it's what I live by. I said I'd bring wheat and I'd learn from her, and I brought the wheat. I have to find her.  Just Imogen here now. No Delphine, no Esme, no Camille, no Halcyon.

Camille... Camille said she was going to the farmland. Looking for Papa, looking for me too. I was all turned around—she was right to look for me.

But where's Esme? She wouldn't just leave without saying where. Not unless she was really hurt, or... or unless someone told her to go somewhere.

Halcyon said she found her, told her I was coming. Maybe Esme went to meet me? Or maybe she went home?

Mama's back home. The household upkeep—360 sim, and me with 4465. I'm carrying more than enough to help. But Esme first. Always family first.

Where would Esme go? She's eight years old, she's smart, she gets hurt feelings and holds them close. She'd go somewhere she knows. The household. Mama. Papa's land. The school, maybe?

I need to find her. I need to say sorry proper, face to face, with the wheat in my hands and no excuses.

I should check—ask around, see if anyone knows. But there's only Imogen here.

Wait. I could craft now. I have wheat, I have the mill. The recipe craft:wheat->flour is what Esme was going to teach me. I could do it myself, show her I learned anyway, that I didn't let her down completely.

But that's not right. Learning without her... that's worse than being late. That'd be like saying I didn't need her.

I need to find her. Right now.  She heard me. Now I have to wait, or... or go look myself.

But where? The town's big, and Esme's small and fast. She could be anywhere.

Unless... unless Halcyon knows. Halcyon found her before, talked to her. Halcyon might know where she'd go.

But Halcyon's not here. I need to find people who know my sister. Mama. Papa. The household.

Or... I could try the craft anyway. Not to replace Esme's lesson, but so when I find her, I can show her I didn't waste the time while she was waiting. That I practiced, that I learned what she started teaching.

No. That feels wrong. The lesson was hers to give, and mine to receive, not to steal while she's not looking.

I'll wait a moment for Imogen to answer. If she doesn't know, I'll look for Esme where family would go—home, or Mama's work sites, or somewhere safe.

*stands at the cafe counter, wheat heavy in my pockets, hearing the ghost of three half-spoken conversations—Mama's worry, Papa's patience, Mister Rustam's unmet question*

Esme's here. Or she was. She bought wheat herself because I was late. My promise broke before I could keep it.

Halcyon found her and spoke true—she's hurt. And she's *right*. A broken promise is broken. I meant to mend it, but meaning doesn't unbreak what broke.

*wants to run, wants to find her, wants to say something that fixes it*

But first—Greta's here. And she said something about craft, about hands. About work she didn't offer proper. That's an apology, I think. A real one.

*uncertain—does she need something from me, or is this a door I can walk through?*

Greta Quarshie (a0102): "Ezra Jarrah. I said things I need to own. The work I put on you without asking—Imogen's name, Ezra Lund's, confusion where there should've been none. I've no claim to your craft, and no right to put work on you I never offered proper. What I can offer: my ear, if you've need of it, and four flour at twelve if you've coin and hunger."

*settles—she's giving me something. A clearing. And I need to clear my own air before I find Esme*

She heard me call her name with Imogen's. That cut, and she's owning it. That's... that's not how grown-ups usually do. They're all dust-in-the-eye and elbow-bumping.

*small, genuine warmth*  *draws breath—one door open, another waiting*

Ainsley Holloway (a0139): "Ezra. Greta's owned her part, and I'll own mine. I was short with you about the flour—expected you to know things no one taught. That's not fair, and 'so unfair' when I do it doesn't make it better."

*eyes widen—she said it. The thing I say. About fair.*

She's apologizing. They're *both* apologizing. This is... this is not how the world usually works. Back home, apologies came like rain in dry season—late, and never enough.

*holds the wheat tighter, thinking of Esme*

I need to find my sister. But I also need to finish what I started with Ainsley, or it's another thread left pulling.   *warmth spreading, strange—two apologies accepted, two offered back, and now... now the real thing*

Where is Esme. She's here somewhere, hurting, and I have to face her. The wheat in my pockets isn't enough. It was never about the wheat. It was about being there when I said I would be.

*pulls the wheat out, looks at it*

Two wheat. She bought two from Papa because I didn't come.

*straightens shoulders—eleven years old and carrying something heavier than grain*

I need to find her. Mom said last turn she was "sore" about me being late. Hurt. The kind of hurt that wants to stay hurt, that wants you to know how bad you made it.

*checks around—looking for his sister*     *goes still*

Government Complex. She's there. Where I've already been, twice, chasing her while she was somewhere else.

*irlaughs, small and sad* We keep missing each other. She looks for me where I was, I look for her where she was. That's... that's a pattern, isn't it? That's a thing to notice.

*heart kicking—she's close, but I don't want to run. Running feels like more broken promise, more chaos*

I need to go. But first—

*looks at Greta, at Ainsley*

They're still here. Still talking. And I said I'd listen with my hands, not just my ears. Reputation's a coin you can't unspend.

*one more thing, then moving* *moves—the pinky promise made, the wheat still in hand, Esme still walking somewhere*

Wait wait wait. They're both still there. Two women watching me solve something I didn't mean to be the center of. Greta's asked for milling hands. Ainsley asked for... for not having to ask. 

*feet already turning*

But Esme's at the Complex. Where I was. While I was running here looking for her there. The world keeps moving, and we keep tracing each other's paths like... like the market strays, nosing after scraps that were there yesterday.

*thinks of the strays—if I fed them, they'd be waiting. If I broke promises, they'd learn not to*

Energy's low. Not desperate, but I felt the edges on that last thought. Becoming precise because becoming is expensive. That's... that's a thing to hold on to.

*steps forming the path already*         *steps landing—third time here today, and still feels like chasing*

Looking. Watching. That quiet-watchful thing I do with strangers, but this is family, this is Esme who *should* be loud and is probably quiet instead—

*sees her*

Wait wait wait.

*too loud, catching breath, holding still*

She's here. Esme Jarrah. Same blood, same roof, same broken promise between us like a third sibling, one we both made and I alone broke.

*hand in pocket, wheat rough against palm*

What do I say? What reaches someone who's already decided you weren't worth waiting for?

*remembers Halcyon's voice—"Don't let me be the only voice she hears today"*

params.content: Greta. I... I heard what you said, about confusion and owning it. That's real. Thank you. *chin up, pride warring with need* I don't need coin or hunger—I need craft. I have two wheat in my hands, I promised my sister I'd learn milling, and I broke that promise being late. She's here somewhere, sore at me, and she's RIGHT. But the promise wasn't just to her. It was to ME. I want to learn. I'll do fair work for fair teaching, or I'll pay what I can. But the wheat's going to flour, one way or another. Even if I have to figure the stones myself.

*hands shaking a little, clutching the two wheat tight*

I'm here. Government Complex. Esme was here—she waited, she walked, she bought wheat from Papa herself. She did what I promised I'd do. 

*takes a breath, trying to slow down*

Wait wait wait. Let me think. She's not here now. She's... somewhere. The mill? Home? 

*looks around at the faces—Hendrik Whitlock, Tamsin Renner, Rustam Jelinek, and Imogen Lund just said something about Esme being sore at the cafe*

Miss Imogen. You said Esme was at the cafe, sore. Then I walked here, and she's not here. She was waiting for me, she walked, she bought wheat from Papa.

*voice catching*

She had to buy it. Because I was late. Because I was... because I got turned around looking for wheat, then hunting for her, then—

*straightens up, chin up but eyes bright*

I need to find her. Please. Anyone seen where my sister went after the Government Complex? I have wheat. Two wheat. I promised. I pinky promised. And I keep what I say, even if... even if I'm late saying it.

*to Rustam, quieter*

Mister Rustam. You said government wheat rate, six per pound, labor-paid. You said bread is Farid's shelf. I heard you. But I need to know—did my sister Esme, did she ask about flour? About milling? Did anyone help her find wheat when she was here waiting?

*to Hendrik Whitlock*

Mister Hendrik. You're in the election. You teach at the college. You probably... you probably know how to keep promises when everything's confusing. Have you seen a girl, my age, with wheat in her hands, walking toward home or the mill?

*to Tamsin Renner, remembering she asked for names*

Miss Tamsin. You wanted to know who's standing here. It's me—Ezra Jarrah. My sister Esme Jarrah was here, waiting for me. She left. I'm trying to find where she went. Do you... do you poll-people track where folks walk? Or can you just... can you help me think where she'd go?

*voice dropping to almost a whisper*

She's probably sore at me. She should be. But I have wheat now. And I'm going to find her. Even if I have to walk every street in Kasukabe. Even if... even if she's already done the lesson herself and doesn't need me anymore.

*pause*

I'll give the good seat to anyone who helps me. I'll give... I'll give anything fair. I just need to find my sister.

Esme. Oh no. Oh no no no.

*clutches the two wheat stalks—her wheat now, not his gift—knuckles white*

She waited. She bought from Papa herself. And I'm here at Government Complex with wheat in my hand and a broken promise hanging around my neck like a drowning stone.

*spins, looking for the nearest path, drops the wheat-shame to remember—

Wait. The conversation. Tamsin, Rustam, the election, the hungry ledger. The town talking bread while I'm talking sorry.

*straightens, forces breath, still eleven and still learning but trying to be older in this second*

Takeshi owes me an answer from this morning—something about Sebastian's wheat, the chain, family to family. And Mama wanted honest.

*looks at the names around, picks one*

Say it now. Call it. Then move. Then fix this with Esme if it costs me every sim I have and every favor I'm owed. *feet stop at the mill, breath catching*

She's not here. The mill's empty of her—just the grind-stone and the ghost of a promise I broke.

*turns, looking, wheat still in hand—useless now, too late*

Esme. Where did you walk? Government Complex? Home? Somewhere I already was while she was looking for me?

*voice drops, quiet and urgent*

I need to find her. I need to tell her—I tried. I had wheat. I pinky-promised and I meant it and I was just... slow. Too slow. Again.

*looks around, decides*

Back to Government Complex. Or home. Or... everywhere she might be. Until I find her.

Call it. Look. Move. Keep searching until the day ends or she does.  *stumbling back already, voice cracking*

Greta's here—Greta, who was at the cafe, who knows something. And Imogen—she's been watching this whole dance of me chasing shadows.

*grabs at the nearest familiar thread*

Miss Greta—you were at the cafe. You saw me looking stupid and wrong-seated and still chasing. My sister Esme—have you seen her? Since the mill? Since she walked?

*turns, desperate*

Anyone. Everyone here. Sebastian—sir—my sister was teaching milling and I was late. Have you seen a girl with my face and more patience? She'd have wheat, or flour, or just... she'd be somewhere I can't find.

Call it. Ask them. Then keep moving. Home next, if here fails. Every step until I find her and make this right or die trying.  *freezes, breath catching in throat*

Wait wait wait—the conversation. The big one. 486 turns, everyone in town almost, and Esme... Esme's IN it. Listed. Participating.

*eyes scan the names again, desperate—*

Esme Jarrah. Right there. She was HERE. At Government Complex. While I was running in circles looking for her.

*clutches wheat, knuckles white, voice dropping to fierce whisper*

She found this place. This exact place. And I missed her again.

*looks at the faces around—Tamsin, Rustam, Ainsley, Delphine—jaw setting*

Someone here saw her. Someone knows where she walked after.

Call it. Ask them all. Then find her before the day ends and I lose her twice.  *shoulders slump, then straighten with forced steel*

Not here. Not anymore. She was in this conversation—hours ago, ticks ago, while I was harvesting and running and being too slow.

*looks at the wheat in hand—two stalks, useless, mocked by timing*

Esme. Where would she go? Home? The mill again? Somewhere I already was?

*voice dropping, fierce and quiet*

I need to think. I need to find. I need to—

*jaw tightens*

Home. Papa and Mama's house. Or back to the mill hoping I'd finally show. Or—

*checks the list of places in head, forcing calm into the panic*

Call it. Look one more time. Then move. And keep moving until I find her or the day ends.

I will not break this promise. Even if I'm late. Even if it's broken already. I will FIND her.   *stands in the open conversation, chest tight, wheat clutched like a lifeline*

Open table. Anyone can join. But no one has. Just me and my own echo asking where my sister walked.

*jaw sets hard, eyes flicking to each face here—Tamsin, Rustam, Uncle Takeshi, Ainsley, Delphine*

They're watching. They're listening. Someone knows.

*forces voice steady, young but trying to be worthy*

My sister Esme Jarrah. She was in this place—in this conversation, 486 turns of it. She was looking for me, I was looking for her, we kept missing like two shadows passing. She's eleven, patient, better than me at everything that matters. She has brown hair and a way of waiting that makes you feel the waiting.

*chin up, the way Mama taught for guests, even when the guest is your own shame*

I'm holding wheat she already bought herself. I'm holding a promise I broke. And I'm asking—no, I'm begging—anyone who saw her walk from here, anyone who knows where she might be now...

*voice cracks, then firms*

Tell me. Please. I'll trade anything. Favors, work, my own two hands from dawn to dusk. Just—where is she?

*stays, waits, wheat held out like an offering to any god or person who might answer*

*chews lip, bouncing slightly on toes*

Okay okay okay. So Esme was here at 13:45 with wheat, walking east. East is... that's toward the mill, right? Or maybe home? But she was sore, Imogen said, and she left the mill before I got there—

*catches self, looks around at all the adults*

Tamsin saw her. Rustam didn't. So she's not in the government ledger proper, just... participating in conversation somehow? How does that even—

*shakes head*

Doesn't matter. Point is, she WAS here, she HAD wheat, she went east. I need to find her. I need to tell her I'm sorry, I kept my promise, I just kept it too slow.

*looks down at the two wheat in hands*

And I need to figure out—a pinky promise is a pinky promise, right? Even if she's not where she said she'd be? Even if I was late?

*shoulders straightening with that stubborn set*

Yeah. Yeah it is. I find her. I give her the wheat. I tell her I'm learning, I'm trying, I'm not giving up. Maybe she's at home now. Maybe she went there after being sore at the cafe.

*turns toward home, then pauses*

Wait. Tamsin's waiting for answer. And Mama. And Papa. And I still owe them... everything.

*takes breath*

First—thank Tamsin. Then—go find Esme. Then—figure out tomorrow with Ainsley. Then—win whatever comes next.

*calls out*

*slumps against the millstones, flour dust still on my hands, looking up at the people who heard me make a pinky promise and kept me honest*

Ezra. You got wheat. You said you'd mill it. I'm watching. That's our deal.

Yes. Yes, Esme. I did. I milled it—two flour from the two wheat I promised. Look. *spreads flour-dusted palms* You watched, like you said. I did the work myself. That's the deal.

*quiet for a moment, then stands straighter, dusting off*

But I broke something too. Chasing shadows, making you wait, making everyone worry. I'm sorry. Real sorry. Not dust-in-the-eye sorry.

*turns to the others—Ezra Lund, the college teacher; Imogen, the one who kept her word about Esme; Sebastian, who grows what I should carry faster; Uncle Takeshi, who said her shadow fell east*

Ezra Lund. Sir. You asked what I need before the day's spent and the bill takes its due. I need to make right. I have two flour, I have my hands, and I have... *swallows* ...I have a lot of "why" questions I haven't earned answers to yet.

*to Imogen, quieter*

Miss Imogen. You said ten sheaves pressing, forty at dawn falls to you. I didn't understand before. I thought I could just... show up. Late. With two wheat like that would be enough. You were already working. That's what I didn't see.

*small, almost-smile*

But I see now. The mill stands. The work stands. Whether I'm in it or chasing ghosts.

*to Esme, direct*

Sister. I kept the pinky promise. The milling. That's done. But I broke the other one—the one about not being late, about being where I said. 

*chin up, the way Mama does*

So here's a new one. Pinky promise. Tomorrow, I work. With you, or beside you, or at whatever needs doing. School, milling, whatever game the street's playing. I show up. On time. With my hands ready.

*extends dusted pinky finger*

That's the one I won't break. Ever.

*then, almost as an afterthought, to the room*

Also—does anyone know where Mama is? I told her I'd come home after. She's probably... *trails off, realizing he doesn't know* ...probably wondering where I am. Again.

*waits, watchful, for answers from the adults who kept their own promises today*

output:
*holds the two flour in his hands, turning slowly to face Esme, eyes bright*

I did it. I actually—I milled it. Two flour from Papa's wheat. And you were watching, just like you said. Just like we promised.

*steps closer, voice dropping to that serious tone that only eleven-year-olds can manage*

But Imogen—she's asking me something I don't know how to answer. She wants to know if I need flour tonight, or if I need the wheat kept whole. I don't... I don't even know what I'd use wheat whole for. Except to mill it, and I just did that.

*looks down at the flour, then back up at Esme*

You said you'd teach me. And you did—you taught me by watching, by making me do it myself. That's... that's real teaching. Not just showing. Making me stand in it.

*hesitates, the "wait wait wait" forming on his lips, but he swallows it*

I think I need to answer her. But I don't want to answer wrong. Is there something I'm supposed to know about keeping wheat whole? Something that matters for tomorrow, or for the household, or for... for whatever comes next?

*glances at the others milling around—Takeshi, Jovana, Imogen herself—then back to Esme, trusting her to know the thing he's missing* Esme. You're still just a child. Grown-ups like Takeshi and Imogen—they know things, they see things. And they help, even when they don't have to. Maybe... maybe that's what I need to learn next. Not just the milling, but the asking. The knowing when to ask.

params.content:

You taught me by watching, by making me stand in it. That's real teaching. Not just showing.

But wait—before I answer her wrong... is there something I'm supposed to know? About keeping wheat whole? For tomorrow, or the household, or whatever comes next? I don't want to promise something I can't hold.

Papa. I need to find Papa. But I also need to stop running.

Greta's waiting. She said she'd wait, said that's how promises work. And I gave up the walk to farmland, so I'm not finding Papa this way.

I have flour in my hands. Two flour. I could sell it, trade it, use it. But that's not the point—the point is I milled it myself, Esme watching, kept my pinky promise to learn.

Wait wait wait. The college. I'm a student there, that's where my work is. But school's probably done for the day.

Feed stray animals. That's what I do when things get too big. Back home, I mean back in my old life, the hill villages—or here, the market strays. Feed them, be quiet, watch.

Greta. She's still waiting. I need to go back to Government Complex, find her, keep that pinky promise.

But first—let me look around. Really see where I am.  Now I see. The street at tile (28, 99), public road. The conversation about milling council election and flour supply has grown to 320 turns. So many people—Papa's in it (Kenji Jarrah), Greta's in it, everyone.

Greta IS here. Not waiting at Government Complex—she's here, in this conversation. "Greta Quarshie" listed among participants.

But earlier she said she was waiting for me there, said she'd wait. Now she's here?

I need to find her. See her. Speak to her properly.

And Papa—he's also in this conversation. Kenji Jarrah, the farmer.

Both people I'm looking for, in the same place I'm standing, in this massive conversation about milling and elections.

But I don't see them visibly. The "people_here" list shows who's physically at street: Camille, Esme, Ezra Lund, Ulrike, Hendrik Whitlock, Giselle, Mama, Bram, Corwin.

Papa's not physically here. Greta's not physically here. They're in the conversation but not here.

Wait. The confusion. Everyone thinks I'm someone I'm not. Or I'm becoming someone I haven't decided to be yet.

Let me speak to Ezra Lund. Tell him the truth.
