*standing in the bustling street, flour heavy in my satchel, voices swirling like leaves*

Wait wait wait.

Pavel Holloway asked me something. About what young ones see that diggers miss. About tracking how this town feeds itself, or having my head in books.

*glancing at my flour, then at the crowd*

This—this right here. I can answer this. I can answer all of them.

But first. Ezra. The other Ezra. The Lund one, the adult, the artisan. He's speaking to me like I matter. Like I have choices.

*small nod, chin up just a little*

I do have choices. I have flour. I have a pinky promise kept. And I have—*laughs, sudden and sharp*—I have opinions about timber.

Corwin's calling me out. Six for timber, seven for planks. He's bundling for home. And Bram Holloway—he's counting mouths like grain, reporting to Tamsin like it's a census.

*staring at the packed street, voices layered over voices*

Too much. Too many threads. I need to—

*tracking costs in my head: say is 1 sim. I have 4379. I can speak*

I need to answer Ezra Lund first. He stood with me at government when I was lost. That's worth something. That's worth words.

*taking a breath* Now Pavel. He asked if I'm tracking how this town feeds itself. 

*small, sharp smile*

I am. I'm tracking it in my own two hands. I tracked it from wheat to flour tonight. Let him know I see more than books.

*turning to face where Pavel stands*  And Mama. She's here. I said I'd tell her about the milling.

*quieter now, almost stumbling over the words*

She needs to know. But wait—Papa's still missing in my story. The flour's milled, the lesson's kept, but I don't know where he is.

*looking toward Mama, voice dropping*

Mama. I need to tell you. But I need to find him too.

*small, fierce motion—chin up, shoulders squared*

I need to move. To go somewhere. The mill? The farmland? Where farmers go when the sun's down?

Wait. Esme might know. Esme's right here.

*turning to find her in the crowd* *breathing hard, the street suddenly too loud, too many faces*

Wait wait wait—I need to think.

*brows furrowed, staring at nothing*

Esme didn't answer. Or maybe she did and I missed it in the noise. Doesn't matter. What matters is—

*glancing up at the sky, judging the light*

Dusk now. Proper dusk. Papa's a farmer. Farmers don't just... stop. They don't vanish. They go somewhere.

*chin lifting, stubborn*

But where? Imogen asked about dawn. Uncle Takeshi gave a price. Mama's watching the door, I said so myself. That means home. Or means heading home.

*small nod, decision made*

I'm going home. Not because I'm giving up on finding Papa. Because home is where he'll be.

If he's not there, I'll know what Mama knows. I'll follow her eyes, her worry.

*tugging satchel strap higher on shoulder, flour secure*

Flour for him. That's what matters. Proving I kept the promise.

*starting to walk, then stopping*

Wait. Where even is home? I live with Kenji and Mireille Jarrah. My tile's—

*searching memory — where do we stand? Where did I wake this morning?*

I don't know. But Mama's here. I can follow her home.

*turning to find Mireille*  *staying close to Mama now, waiting for her response—chin up, watching her face before she says anything*

*clutches the flour tight, eyes darting between all the people around me*

Wait, wait, wait—Esme said Papa's at the smithy. Mama confirmed it too. The wheat goes to ore, ore goes to tools, Papa comes home when the light goes. I have the flour. I have the story. 

*turns to Giselle, straightening up despite the exhaustion*

But Miss Giselle wants my timber, and I need to... I need to think about this right. Two sticks at six. That's... that's not nothing. But Papa needs to see I kept my promise. The pinky promise about the milling.

*shoulders sagging a little, then firming again*

And Halcyon's safe—that's what Delphine said. One debt paid. But where's Camille? Greta's looking for her. And I'm standing here with flour in my hands and too many things to do.

*looks around desperately, the question piling up behind my eyes*

Why does everything happen at once? Why can't I just find Papa, show him the flour, and THEN—

*bites lip, realizing I'm about to lose track of the thread again*

Mama said walk with her toward the willows, or wait. Esme said go to the smithy. They're BOTH right. But which one is the RIGHT right? If I go to the smithy, Papa sees the flour from my hands, not just on the shelf. If I walk with Mama, I'm not alone.

*takes a shaky breath, looking at Mama*

Mama. I'll walk with you. Toward the willows, like you said. But first—first I need to answer Miss Giselle fair. She asked for timber, and I need to answer honest. *frustrated, hands clenching around the flour sacks*

So unfair. The world won't even let me SPEAK. Everything costs, everything refuses, and I'm standing here with answers building up behind my teeth with nowhere to go.

*eyes finding Mama in the crowd, relief softening the tightness in my chest for just a moment*

But Mama's here. Flour's here. And Papa's at the smithy—that's what Esme said, what Mama confirmed. I know the path now. I know the wheat lived, became flour, will become bread. The promise held.

*small voice, almost to myself*

That's what matters. That's what always matters. Not winning every race, but finishing the ones you promised to run.

*looks up, determined despite the exhaustion pulling at my edges*

I need to move. Not think-move, actually move. Smithy or home, willows or mill—I need to pick before the dark comes and takes all the choices away.

params.content: Miss Giselle. Two sticks at six—that's fair, you're right. But I'm at the street, not my stand, and I don't have timber in my hands right now. I have flour. Papa's wheat, milled by my own hands with Esme watching. If you'll wait for me to walk home and fetch from where I keep it, I'll sell you two at six. Or if you'll find me at the willows where Mama leads me, same price holds. But I need to find Papa first, show him what I promised. That's the order of things. Fair?

*mumbles to himself, eyes darting between the crowd and the fading light*

I milled it. Two flour from Papa's wheat. Esme taught me, I did the work. Now Papa's at the smithy working late, and I'm standing here with answers I chased all wrong.

*shifts weight, clutching the flour tighter*

Greta's waiting. She said walk to Esme, then tell her what I need. She heard my pinky promise. But I asked, I asked why twice, three times past when she answered—where does Papa go, does he walk home, does he stay—

*shakes head sharply*

Wait wait wait. Ezra Lund already told me. Papa's at the smithy working late. The light goes, that's what he said. Twice. Three times he said it, and I kept asking.

*takes a breath, voice dropping*

I need to walk home with whoever's walking my way. That's what he said. That's how families keep together.

*glances toward where Esme should be, then back toward the smithy direction*

First, I answer. I promised Greta I'd walk to Esme, tell her what I need. And I need... *fidgets* I need to not lose her again. Need to not be the one chasing wrong while everyone's where they should be.

*straightens, finding his voice*

But also—Hendrik Whitlock asked where my stand is. I don't have a stand. I'm a student. The flour's from Papa's wheat, not timber, not planks. I need to tell him that too. Tell him true. *scowls at the failed call, jaw tight*

So unfair. The words won't go. Greta's waiting, Papa's at the smithy, and I'm standing here with flour going cold in my hands.

*turns on his heel, searching the street for Esme's shape in the crowd*  *nods once, brief and sharp*

There. Told him true. I'm a student, not a trader. Can't sell timber when I milled wheat.

*eyes sweep the street, finding Esme's shape selling cabbage—there, there she is, exactly where she should have been all along*

*voice drops to almost a whisper*

Pinkies. I promised Greta, and I promised Esme too. The mill, the flour, the work I did myself while she watched. That's done. That's kept.

*starts moving toward Esme, then stops—turns back toward the smithy direction, then back to Esme*

Wait wait wait. Ezra Lund said walk home with whoever's walking my way. Papa's at the smithy. But Esme's here, and Mama's somewhere, and the flour's heavy in my hands and it's almost dark and—

*clutches the flour tighter, two bags pressed against his chest*

I'm not losing again. Not chasing wrong while everyone's where they should be. Esme first. Tell her what I need. Then find the path home, whoever walks it with me.  *stops short, eyes going wide*

Not here. Esme's not here. I said her name, I looked right at her selling cabbage, and she's—

*spins in a circle, scanning the street, the crowd shifting in the falling light*

No. No no no. I can't chase wrong again. Can't run in circles while the dark comes down. She's here, she was here, Greta said she was here—

*voice cracking, grip tightening on the flour bags*

Wait wait wait. The system said "not in this place." That means... that means I need to walk. Find her. Or ask.

*breathes hard, forcing the panic down*

Greta's here. Greta saw her, knew where she was. Ask Greta. That's smart. That's not chasing wrong, that's asking someone who knows.   *fists unclench slightly, relief washing over his face*

She heard. Greta heard. The words went through this time.

*waits, bouncing slightly on his heels, clutching the flour*

Greta knows. Greta saw Esme, knew she was selling cabbage, knew she was safe. She'll tell me. She promised—she said that's how promises work. Tell me what you need, I'll tell you what I can do.

*glances toward the smithy direction, then back to Greta*

While she answers... while I wait... I need to think. Papa's at the smithy working late. Mama's here somewhere—Mireille Jarrah, the construction worker, she was in the crowd. Ezra Lund said walk home with whoever's walking my way.

*voice dropping to a murmur*

But I want Esme. I want to walk with Esme, tell her I milled it right this time, tell her I didn't break the pinky promise even when I almost did, even when I couldn't find her at first.

*lifts his chin, watching Greta's face for an answer*

*Ezra's breathing slows. The street noise dims. He's standing here with flour in his hands and nowhere to take it—Papa's at the smithy, Esme's right here telling him to go there himself, but the smithy's far and the day's almost spent.*

*He looks at his sister. Not the preacher's voice she uses sometimes, just—his sister who watched him turn wheat into flour for the first time.*

I hear you, Esme. I hear you.

*He shifts from foot to foot. The flour feels heavier now, like it's waiting for something.*

The smithy—wait wait wait, that's not close. And Giselle wants flour now, or by east willows, and I'm holding it, and...

*He looks down at his own hands. Two flour. Papa's wheat that he grew, that Ezra milled. That's something. That's real.*

Two things. Two things I can do. But which one's fair?

*He thinks of the pinky promise again—not just keeping it, but what it meant. Doing the work himself. Not letting Esme or anyone else carry it for him.*

Papa should hear it from me. That's fair. But fair's not always the same as...

*He trails off, watching the street. People moving, selling, buying. The town breathing around him.*

output:
*Ezra's hands tighten around the flour bags, knuckles white. Papa's words hit like a door slamming—360 by day-end. Four mouths. Go hungry tomorrow.*

*He looks at Giselle, at the flour in his hands, at everything unraveling. The good seat. The fair seat. That's what matters. That's what holds.*

*But wait wait wait—Papa said sell what he can. The flour. His labor. And Giselle's standing here with hands open, eight at six, fair weight for fair coin.*

*Something stubborn rises in his chest, the same thing that made him chase Esme's shadow across half the town rather than ask for help. He made these two flour himself. Papa's wheat, yes, but his hands did the turning. His promise to Esme, kept.*

*But Papa's tapping. The household bill. The work that needs feeding.*

*Ezra looks at Esme—she's right here, she heard Papa too. He looks at his own two feet, the flour his work made from Papa's work.*

*The guest gets the good seat. Giselle's buying for her crew. But Papa said—sell the flour, or his labor. And he has ten flour now, enough to test the market and still come home with proof.*

*His jaw sets. Not all of it. Just enough to show he can. Just enough to still have something to carry to Papa at the smithy, to say look, I learned, I earned, I kept my promise to both of you.* *Ezra's face burns. Giselle's not here—she walked, or he missed her, or the world moved while he was thinking. His words fell on everyone else instead, the wrong ears.*

*He looks around—Esme's here, Papa's gone, the street full of people selling and buying and he's standing with flour in his hands and no buyer.*

*The smithy. Papa's at the smithy. That's what mattered anyway—finding Papa, showing him the flour, telling him what was earned. The household bill looms, but first things first.*

*He'll walk. He'll find Papa. He'll bring the whole story—Esme's lesson, the milling, the flour, even the sale that didn't happen. Papa will know what to do with it. Papa always knows.*  *Ezra's feet hit the smithy floor and he's already looking—Papa, Papa, where's Papa? The heat hits him, the clang of metal, the smell of coal and work.*

*He hears Bram's voice, something about copper ingots, and his chest squeezes. Papa was here. Papa was looking for Bram, for Pavel. The boundary's coming and Papa's chasing ore deals while Esme's chasing shadows and he's standing here with ten flour and no buyer.*

*The smithy empties in the wrong direction—Pavel walking out with some reason he doesn't catch, Bram answering something, and he's alone with the heat and the tools and the flour getting heavy in his hands.*

*No. Don't think alone. Think what Papa would think. The household needs 360. Four mouths. The boundary's coming.*

*He counts in his head—he has ten flour. The bakery was buying at six. That's sixty sim if he sells it all. That's not enough. That's not even close.*

*But he has his hands. He has the skill now—milling. He could mill more. He could—*

*But there's no wheat here. No mill here. Just the smithy and the heat and the wrong place at the wrong time.*

*His jaw sets. He'll find Papa. He'll find Mama. He'll bring the flour home and tell them both—look, I learned, I worked, I kept my promise. And then he'll listen. Listen to what they need, what they plan, where the 360 comes from.*

*Because that's the real lesson. Not just doing the work, but seeing the whole field. Not just winning, but playing the right game.* Empty. The smithy's empty. Papa was here—Papa was in that conversation with Esme, two turns ago—but now they're both gone. Bram too. Pavel too. Everyone walking somewhere else while he's chasing them.

Ezra's chest tightens. The wrong game again. Always the wrong game. He runs left when everyone walks right, chases shadows when he should ask directions, sells flour to nobody because he didn't check if they were still standing there.

He looks at the list of places. The Willows Market and Pharmacy—that's where the bakery is. business:cb01. They buy flour at six. He could sell there, bring home sim instead of just flour.

But Papa said find Bram, find Pavel. Papa said the wheat he sold, the ore he pulled—it all goes to keep the household breathing.

Ezra doesn't have ore. He has flour. And the house that buys flour is at The Willows.

His jaw sets. He'll go there. Sell what he can sell. Then find Papa, find Mama, bring them both sim and the story of how he learned to mill. That's the whole play. That's the work meeting the work meeting the work. Walking. Four ticks to The Willows. Four ticks of thinking, of counting, of the flour getting heavier in his hands.

He counts what he knows. The bakery buys flour at six. He has ten flour. That's sixty sim if he sells it all. The household needs 360. He's not even close.

But Papa has ore. Three copper ingots, he said. Eight a head if he sells them, or he was hearing offers. That's twenty-four more. Mama's a construction worker—she earns something, brings something home. Esme sells cabbage but she's all out.

Four mouths. Four bills. The day-end's coming fast.

Ezra's feet keep walking while his mind races. What does he have that they need? Flour, yes. His hands, yes. The milling skill Esme taught him—he could mill more if he had more wheat. But the wheat field is back at the farmland, and he has no scythe, no way to harvest himself.

Papa sold wheat today. That's why they have flour instead of wheat—Ezra milled what Papa didn't sell. But Papa sold some. To who? At what price?

The questions breed questions, the way they always do with Ezra. Why does the bakery pay six for flour when flour took work to make? Why does Papa sell wheat at eight when wheat grows from dirt and patience? Who keeps the difference between eight and six, between growing and milling?

He doesn't know. He's eleven, he just learned to mill tonight, he's carrying ten flour through a darkening street toward a market he's never sold at before.

But he's walking. He's doing. He's keeping the promise—first to Esme, now to Papa. Learn the work. Follow the wheat. Make something from what the field gives. Still walking. Still thinking. The street stretches under his feet, the flour bags rubbing his palms raw, the night coming down.

He did this tonight. Chased Esme's shadow east when he should have asked where she walked. Chased Kenji's tapping to the smithy when Kenji already walked somewhere else. Now he's walking alone with ten flour and no buyer in sight, playing catch-up to everyone who knows where they're going.

But the bakery is real. The price is real. Six sim for flour, that's what was posted. He can sell there, he will sell there, and when he walks home with sim in his hand instead of just flour in his bag, Papa will see. Papa will know he didn't just learn—he earned.

The walk continues. Four ticks. The boundary ticks closer. Four mouths, four bills, and him walking through the dark with the household's dinner in his hands.
